verification.status: 'verified' = checked against a news or government source on compiled_on; 'schedule_based' = date derived from the body's standing schedule, not a posted agenda; 'illustrative' = realistic placeholder for the demo — replace with the real posted agenda before showing it as fact.

civic_items.title: Last day to register to vote for the November 3 election
civic_items.summary_plain: Today is the deadline to register or update your address so you can vote on November 3. If you've moved since the last election, update your registration so you get the right ballot.
civic_items.location: Online at the Secretary of the Commonwealth's website, or your city or town clerk

civic_items.title: Deadline to request a mail-in ballot
civic_items.summary_plain: Your request for a mail-in ballot has to reach your local election office by October 27. After that, plan to vote early in person or on Election Day.

civic_items.title: Early in-person voting is open
civic_items.summary_plain: Early voting started October 17. You can vote in person before Election Day at your town's early voting locations; hours vary by town.
civic_items.location: Your city or town's early voting sites

civic_items.title: State election — November 3, 2026
civic_items.summary_plain: Election Day. Along with candidates, Massachusetts voters will decide nine statewide ballot questions, tying the state's record from 1994.

civic_items.title: Question 1: Apply the public records law to the Legislature and governor's office
civic_items.summary_plain: Right now the Legislature is fully exempt from the public records law, and the governor's office has claimed an exemption. This question would make most of their records requestable by the public, while still letting them withhold communications about helping constituents and developing policy.
civic_items.yes_means: The Legislature and governor's office would be covered by the public records law, with some exceptions.
civic_items.no_means: The Legislature stays exempt, and the governor's office can keep claiming an exemption.

civic_items.title: Question 2: Let public defender office staff unionize
civic_items.summary_plain: Employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services, the state's public defender agency, can't currently bargain collectively. This would let them form a union and negotiate pay, benefits, leave, and working conditions.
civic_items.yes_means: CPCS employees could form a union and collectively bargain.
civic_items.no_means: CPCS employees still couldn't collectively bargain.

civic_items.title: Question 3: Replace party primaries with one all-party primary
civic_items.summary_plain: Starting in 2028, every candidate for state office would run in one shared primary, and the top two vote-getters would advance to November — even if they're from the same party.
civic_items.yes_means: One all-party primary; the top two finishers advance to the general election, starting in 2028.

civic_items.title: Question 4: Allow voter registration on Election Day
civic_items.summary_plain: Today you have to register 10 days before an election. This would let eligible residents register and vote at their polling place on Election Day, and let registered voters update their address there (but not their party).
civic_items.yes_means: Same-day registration at the polls on Election Day.

civic_items.title: Question 5: Change the state tax revenue cap and rebates
civic_items.summary_plain: Massachusetts already limits how much tax revenue it can keep, and refunds the excess. This would base the cap on last year's actual revenue (grown by wage growth) instead of last year's cap, and count millionaire's-surtax revenue toward it — making taxpayer rebates more likely.
civic_items.yes_means: A tighter cap formula; the state would owe rebates more often.

civic_items.title: Question 6: Dedicated conservation fund from sporting goods sales tax
civic_items.summary_plain: This would send up to $100 million a year of the existing sales tax collected on sporting goods into a new natural resource conservation fund, overseen by a 15-member board. It doesn't add a new tax; the Legislature would still control spending.
civic_items.yes_means: Creates the fund and routes that sales tax revenue to it.
civic_items.no_means: Conservation stays in the regular budget; the revenue stays in the General Fund.

civic_items.title: Question 7: Allow single-family homes on smaller lots
civic_items.summary_plain: On lots with public water and sewer, towns couldn't require more than 5,000 square feet of land or 50 feet of street frontage to build a single-family home. Supporters say it enables cheaper 'starter homes'; it would take some lot-size decisions away from towns.
civic_items.yes_means: A statewide cap on minimum lot size (5,000 sq ft) and frontage (50 ft) where public water and sewer exist.

civic_items.title: Question 8: Repeal recreational marijuana sales
civic_items.summary_plain: This would undo the recreational part of the 2016 law that legalized cannabis. Retail shops would have to become medical dispensaries or sell to one; medical marijuana would continue. Adults with one to two ounces could face a $100 fine.
civic_items.yes_means: Ends recreational marijuana sales; medical stays.
civic_items.no_means: Licensed recreational sales to adults 21+ continue.

civic_items.title: Question 9: Keep or repeal the 2024 gun law
civic_items.summary_plain: A referendum on the gun law passed in 2024, which covers ghost guns and 3-D printed guns, expands the 'red flag' law, and broadens the assault weapon definition. Because it's a referendum on an existing law, a YES vote keeps the law.
civic_items.yes_means: Keeps the 2024 gun law in place.

verification.note: One outlet described YES as repeal; YES = keep matches how MA veto referendums are worded. Confirm against the official ballot wording.

civic_items.title: Statewide school cellphone policy (An Act to promote student learning and mental health)
civic_items.summary_plain: Would require every public school district to adopt and enforce a policy limiting student cellphone use during the school day. The Senate passed it in July 2025; the House hasn't agreed on a final version, and lawmakers have until early January 2027 to make a deal.

status_history.action: Still unresolved between House and Senate (reported)

civic_items.title: An Act to Promote Yes in My Backyard (YIMBY bill)
civic_items.summary_plain: A broad zoning reform bill meant to make it easier to build housing. The House didn't act after a September hearing. The Senate committee advanced an amended version in December, but it has sat in Senate Ways and Means since. Its duplex provision was moved into the economic development bill.

civic_items.title: Economic development bill: duplexes by right, faith-based housing, tenant right to purchase
civic_items.summary_plain: The House and Senate passed different versions and are negotiating. Proposals include allowing duplexes anywhere single-family homes are allowed (Senate), letting religious institutions build affordable multifamily housing on their land (House), and giving tenants a right to match an offer to buy their building (both). Deadline to finish: January 5, 2027.

civic_items.title: Zoning variance reform (in the FY2027 state budget) — now law
civic_items.summary_plain: Makes it easier for local zoning boards to grant exceptions for housing: the standard drops from 'substantial hardship' to 'practical difficulty', boards can weigh the public need for housing, and approvals last two years instead of one.

status_history.action: Signed by Governor Healey; effective immediately

civic_items.title: Sales tax exemption for multifamily construction materials — now law
civic_items.summary_plain: Building materials for multifamily housing are exempt from sales tax when the project is in a lower-income census tract (median income under 120% of area median) or at least 15% of units are income-restricted.

civic_items.title: Study single-stair apartment buildings
civic_items.summary_plain: Would study when small apartment buildings with one staircase (common in Europe, cheaper to build) should be allowed. The bill is parked in Ways and Means, but the governor created an advisory group based on it by executive order.

civic_items.title: Accessory dwelling unit (ADU) trust fund
civic_items.summary_plain: Would create a state fund to help homeowners build backyard or in-law apartments. Reported favorably by the Housing committee but hasn't moved out of Ways and Means.

civic_items.title: Energy affordability bill
civic_items.summary_plain: The House and Senate passed different energy bills and are still negotiating. One major difference: the House version would cut the Mass Save efficiency program's budget by about $1 billion.
